core: Definition of supply as the whole relationship between price and quantity supplied (a schedule/curve), not a single amount

Law of supply: ceteris paribus, a higher price raises quantity supplied and a lower price lowers it, giving an upward-sloping supply curve, and WHY (higher price makes additional output more profitable)
Supply schedule (table) versus supply curve (graph) as two views of the same relationship
Quantity supplied (one point at one price) versus supply (the entire curve)
Movement ALONG the supply curve (driven by the good's own price) versus a SHIFT of the whole curve (driven by determinants)
Determinants that shift supply: input/factor prices, technology, number of sellers, seller expectations of future prices, taxes and subsidies, and prices of related goods in production
supporting: Ceteris paribus assumption and its limits
Direction of a shift: rightward = increase in supply (more at every price), leftward = decrease
Illustrative gasoline supply schedule from OpenStax
outOfScope: Market equilibrium where supply meets demand (economics:foundations:market-equilibrium)
Production functions and firm cost curves (economics:foundations:production, economics:foundations:costs)

claims.claim: Supply is the amount of a good or service a producer is willing and able to offer at each price; it is the whole price-quantity relationship (a schedule or curve), not one number.
The law of supply states that, holding other factors constant, a rise in price almost always increases the quantity supplied and a fall in price decreases it, so the supply curve slopes upward.
Quantity supplied refers to a single point on the supply curve (one quantity at one price), whereas supply refers to the entire curve or schedule.

In OpenStax's illustrative gasoline supply schedule, quantity supplied rises from 500 million gallons at $1.00 per gallon to 720 million gallons at $2.20 per gallon (with intermediate points 550, 600, 640, 680, and 700).
A change in the good's own price causes a movement along a fixed supply curve (a change in quantity supplied); it does not shift the curve.
A shift in supply means a change in the quantity supplied at every price, caused by a non-price factor; a rightward shift is an increase in supply and a leftward shift is a decrease.
Lower input/factor prices reduce the cost of production and shift supply to the right; higher input costs shift it to the left.
A cost-reducing technological improvement shifts the supply curve to the right because the same inputs now produce more output.
Taxes and many regulations raise production costs and shift supply left, while subsidies lower costs and shift supply right.
An increase in the number of sellers supplying a good shifts the supply curve to the right; a reduction in the number of sellers shifts it to the left.

Seller expectations about future prices affect current supply, and when a producer can make substitutes in production, a rise in the price of one shifts supply of the other to the left as resources are redirected.
